Canadian Camping 







CAM PENG — 


Mountain Style 


“When it’s Springtime in the Rockies” 
may be just a song to you, but to 
hundreds of Alberta boys and girls 
ihat’s one of the many times their 
memories turn to camping at Holiday 
House, Camp Chief Hector or Camp 
Inuspi — three truly mountain-style 
camps. 

On the outskirts of Banff, the Beauti¬ 
ful, near the famous Cave and Basin, 
is located the Calgary Y.W.C.A. girls’ 
camp—Holiday House. Built originally 
as a millionaire’s mansion, it has been 
adapted to camp life very successfully 
with but one major drawback. When 
vou think of camp you always think 
of campfires, but National Park regula¬ 
tions prohibit campfires except for very 
special occasions. They always manage 
to have at least one during each ten- 
day camp period, and the huge fireplace 
in the lodge provides a cheery back¬ 
ground for many programs which would 
ordinarily be held outside. Ploliday 
House has many unique attractions— 
rwimming at the heated pool, two 
hundred yards up the road; bears, 
moose and deer “dropping in” to look 
things over; a dining hall with murals 
painted by a famous artist; and tiled 
bathtubs with lots of hot water to re¬ 
lax vour weary bones after a strenuous 
mountain climb or a bike trip around 
the Banff Springs Golf Course. Pro¬ 
gram at Holiday House features music, 
crafts, cycling, mountain climbing, na- 
mre clubs, etc., and special evenings 
when guests from the Banff School of 
Fine Arts or local Naturalists, give 
presentations. 


During the five years Holiday House 
has been open, many business girls, as 
well as school girls, have enjoyed its 
facilities and program, and many are 
the amateur puppeteers in Calgary and 
district who became fascinated with 
the little moppets there. 

Impossible to achieve a real camp 
atmosphere under such conditions, you 
say? Well—they may miss out on a 
few traditional camp features, but by 
and large, the girls have as fine a camp 
experience at Holiday House as any¬ 
where. 

Thirty miles south of Holiday House, 
just off the Banff highway, the 
Y.M.C.A.’s Camp Chief Hector, for 
boys of Calgary and district, nestles in 
the “Evening shadow of the Rockies”. 
Situated on the Stoncy Indian Reserve, 
the camp boasts one of the few warm- 
water lakes in the mountains, Lake 
Bowfort, and rising from the shores of 
the lake opposite the campsite, tower 
the giants of the Fairholmc Range— 
Yam Nuska, End Mountain and Asso¬ 
ciation. These are the goals of many 
mountain climbing parties who spend 
at least one day each week scaling the 
peaks. On the “flats” south of camp 
are excellent hiking areas for the 
younger boys, and many fine pony trails. 
The lake itself—about one mile long 
and three-quarters of a mile wide—pro¬ 
vides fine swimming, boating and 
canoeing, with the thrill of sailing—a 
goal for which the seniors strive. Three- 
day canoe trips south to the Ghost 
River, ‘and mountain trips to distant 
peaks, provide a real challenge to older 
boys. 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1950 


7 



Gamp Chief Hector, is famous for its 
Indian traditions — named for the 
Stoney Chief who negotiated with 
Y.M.C.A. officials in 1929 for the use 
of the campsite. The present Chief and 
many of his men are familiar and wel¬ 
come guests at the camp. Here the boys 
sleep in the traditional Indian tepees, 
and the Stoneys claim that the Council 
Tepee is the largest in the world! 
Grand Indian Councils, Indian contests 
and pow-wows highlight camp program, 
while the Calgary Stampede has noth¬ 
ing to better the annual Stampede at 
Camp Hector. 

A strange sight amid the tall pine 
trees at Camp Hector is an old Calgary 
street car—remodelled into a fine craft 
shop. For here as at Holiday House 
and Camp Inuspi crafts are an impor¬ 
tant camp experience. 

Further south in beautiful Waterton 
Lakes National Park is the camp of 
the Lethbridge Y.M.C.A., Camp Inus¬ 
pi, or “Camp of the Long Hair”, 
named after historic Kootenay Brown 
who had a trading post in the early 
days on the camp property. Indian 
pony races were held on the camp 
flats in front of the present dining 
lodge, so here, too, the traditions of the 
Red Man are observed and closely in¬ 
corporated into camp program. This 
past summer the camp had the mis¬ 
fortune to lose its dining lodge by fire, 
but nothing daunted, the camp carried 
on, using a large marquee as temporary 
quarters. 

Camp Inuspi is also fortunate in 
having a small lake all to itself—Knight 
Lake—which is separated from the 
main Waterton Lakes by a small stream 
known as Stony Creek. Fishing is a 
popular program feature at Inuspi, and 
many are the lively brook trout which 
fall to the lure of young fishermen and 
women; for Camp Inuspi is unique, too, 
in that its facilities are used by both 
boys and girls—three weeks for boys 
and three to four weeks for girls. Many 


young adult groups, both from the 
Y.M.C.A. and local organizations, have 
enjoyed co-ed weekend camps at 
Inuspi. 

Mountain climbing, swimming, crafts 
and Indian ceremonies play an impor¬ 
tant part in the program here too, and 
the staff at Camp Inuspi has used to 
great advantage members of the 
National Parks Staff, -who willingly 
participate in programs specializing in 
nature lore and camp craft. 

There are many excellent mountains 
to climb, with Vimy Mt. rising eight 
hundred and fifty feet immediately 
behind the camp. Red Rock Canyon, 
a favourite spot for tourists, and Crypt 
Lake, provide good climbing and 
camping. 

Mountain camps are not so very- 
different from other types of camps, but 
they do offer thrills and challenges not 
met elsewhere—although the story is 
told of one of the Holiday House girls 
from Regina who was persuaded by her 
enthusiastic mountain-loving camp 
mates to arise in the wee sma’ hours of 
the morning and climb Sulphur Moun¬ 
tain, to see the sun rise. Lying on the 
top of the mountain, she sleepily 
watched the majestic sight of the sun 
coming up between two distant moun¬ 
tain peaks and grumblingly remarked: 
“Heck! I could see the same sight for 
lots less effort lying on a Saskatchewan 
prairie watching the sun rise between 
two stooks of grain!” 


“The future of the race marches for¬ 
ward on the feet of children.” 

—Phillips Brooks.

Canadian Camping 



ANH WHAT IT MEANS 


A great step forward in the field of 
organized camping in Canada took 
place when, through the efforts and per¬ 
sistence of a group of social-welfare 
minded Canadian men and women 
—camping pioneers—a new constitu¬ 
tion was drafted in a form acceptable 
for Incorporation by the Secretary of 
State for Canada. 

What Does Incorporation 
Mean: 

il) That the C.C.A. has established 
its existence in a form approved 
by the law. 

<2) That the C.C.A. now possesses a 
legal personality apart from any of 
its members-—which is one of the 
prerequisites of recognition by 
many governmental departments 
and other money-granting agen¬ 
cies. 

4 3) That the C.C.A. as a legal person 
has rights, powers and privileges 
apart from those who administer 
its affairs; it can thus follow and 
carry out any of the objects enu¬ 
merated below in its own right 
through its constitutionally ap¬ 
pointed administrators. 

4) That the By-laws of the C.C.A. 
set out the regulations governing 
its operations and through a demo¬ 
cratic procedure. 

5) That the qualifications, powers, 
duties and responsibilities of the 
Officers and Directors of the 
C.C.A. are clearly defined by its 
By-laws. 

5) That the_ spheres of activity of the 
C.C.'A. tod of its committees are 
defined in its Objects and By-laws. 


To Sum Up: The Incorporation of 
the Canadian Camping Association 
means that it now exists in a form 
recognized by the State as being the 
most satisfactory for its continued exis¬ 
tence and democratic functioning. 

Copies of the new C.C.A. Constitu¬ 
tion may be obtained by writing to the 
National Office. The Executive of the 
C.C.A. recommends that every Provin¬ 
cial Association adopt a Constitution 
or revise its present one. It will be 
only too happy to help and advise. 

Canadian Camping 
Association Objects 

(a) To further the interests and wel¬ 
fare of children, youth and adults 
through camping as an educative, 
character building and construc¬ 
tive recreational experience; 

(b) To act as a co-ordinating body 
for camping throughout Canada; 

(c) To .develop and encourage high 
standards in camping and the 
maintenance thereof; 

(d) To study all aspects of camping 
and to interpret and disseminate 
knowledge concerning develop¬ 
ments and regulations pertaining 
thereto; 

(f) To acquire and own assets, prop¬ 
erty, privileges, real estate and 
other rights by purchase, donation 
or legacy for the purpose of the 
Association; to sell, alienate, and 
exchange the said properties and 
to^cquire-other properties in their 
place. 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1950 


9 


Goals For WHO 

At a meeting of the Board, held in 
Ottawa in November, it was decided 
that while the general objectives set 
out in the Preamble to the Constitution 
were splendid, the C.C.A. should 
choose a few particular goals for 1950. 
At the end of the year it would be 
possible to evaluate the results of the 
efforts and analyze the weaknesses. 
This met with the enthusiastic support 
of the Board and the following Goals 
are listed in priority of importance: 

1. That office facilities be established 
for the National Executive to pro¬ 
vide efficient means of communica¬ 
tion between: 

’ The C.C.A. and Provincial Sections 
The Provincial Sections 
Cooperating Agencies 
Individuals and the C.C.A. 

2. To discover the implications of 
the new Charter and to follow 
meticulously the rtiles set out by 
the Constitution. 

Models of existing Provincial Con¬ 
stitutions would be exchanged and 
reviewed to make certain they 
were in order with the new Con¬ 
stitution and to assist those pro¬ 
vinces desiring to set up new con¬ 
stitutions. 

Copies of the Charter to be sent to 
Presidents, Executives and Board 
Members. 

3. To increase membership, by at 
least fifty members, the new rou¬ 


tines set up for the Membership 
Committee to be followed. 

4. To define the aims and objectives 
of good camping, the Public Rela¬ 
tions Committee to be responsible 
for circulating this among the 
members and to seek opportunities 
to publish articles, interpreting 
camping to the public, printed in 
newspapers and magazines. 

5. To prepare a Camp Directory of 
all Canadian camps in two sec¬ 
tions : 

(a) All camps, members of the 
'C.C.A. 

(b) All other camps. 

6. To assist provincial associations to 
obtain leaders and speakers for 
regional conferences and seminars. 

7. To work toward better standards 
by securing and disseminating ma¬ 
terial through the Committee on 
Standards. 

8. To explore the possibilities of hav¬ 
ing the Dominion government 
build camps for children in nation¬ 
al parks and these camps available 
on a rental basis to agencies. 

9. To present a bibliography of camp 
material in various fields for the 
use of the members of the C.C.A. 

10. To promote international aware¬ 
ness in our camps through greater 
knowledge of the responsibilities 
of Canadian and National Citizen¬ 
ship.

Canadian Camping 



THE StSSJKS 



Joyce M. Tyrrell, 


Assistant Director of Swimming and Water Safety, 
Ontario Division, Canadian Red Cross. 



Can we make campers “safety con- 
oks" without at the same time mak- 
-325 them into “sissies”? Is it possible 
^srround boys and girls with all the 
2 src 2 .utions necessary to safe camping 
rd»ut taking from them the incen- 
for initiative, self reliance and 
which make up the great ad- 
of outdoor living? 

This is a problem which every Gamp 
i trrctor answers intentionally or unin- 
32333Dnally when he chooses a camp 
■ 33 f_ lays out a waterfront, hires staff 
-cd formulates camp rules; his policy 
then be reflected in the smaller 
-n-cirions made by counselors in dealing 
vsl* the campers themselves. It may 
«rr =2 presumptious, therefore, for any- 
itat other than a Camp Director to 
recess safety regulations in a camp, 
■« through my work with the Red 
'Zcse-n Water Safety Programme I have 
Trra forced to try to clarify my own 
rtrtking on the matter for the sake of 
me Instructors-in-training, who attend 
-or Courses and who are puzzled by 
mr problem. I offer these suggestions 
=. the hope that they may prove useful 
m c«hcrs. , 

I cannot forget that these young men 
~ad women will soon be responsible 
x* the lives of many people at pools, 
■•rscbcs. and in our camps. I am glad 
through Red Cross training, we 
tsa help them to keep their waterfronts 
tnr from accidents, even if sometimes 
me price of this safety must include 
cijccnc rules and strict regimentation. 

Often some members of the Instruc- 
rsr* Course—usually ones with camp- 
ms experience—are not satisfied with 


this emphasis on safety alone. “Such 
a lot of rules takes all the fun out of 
camping,” they complain. “Kids who 
think of their own safety all the time 
have no spunk”. 

Is it possible to over-emphasizc safety 
regulations? This is a fair question 
which should be fairly answered by 
those of us whose business it is to 
“teach safety”. I think then of a little 
girl who came straight from New York 
to one of our Northern camps and who 
went in my charge on her first long 
hike. Never shall I forget that child’s 
response when we came upon a lovely 
little lake hidden deep in the woods 
and she and her companions could 
shed their clothes and plunge straight 
into the cool waters. She was almost 
beside herself with the beauty and 
freshness of it all. Some years later 
I met her again and she still remem¬ 
bered. I feel sure that any outward 
sign of regimentation at that time 
would have spoiled something that was 
perfect for her. In this particular case 
my group was so small that I could 
watch them without seeming to do so, 
and therefore the risk was slight. But 
whether the group is large or small I 
believe that the question remains the 
same and that the answer must always 
be a positive one. 

Children will sense what is expected 
of them more easily than they will read 
lists of rules or even listen to good 
advice. Think, for instance, how hard 
it is to obey a red traffic light and stay 
on the curb when everyone else is 
wandering out into the road but how 


- srwto, Canada, February, 1950 


11 



easy it becomes when the whole crowd 
is patiently obeying the signal. Hence, 
when young campers see counselors and 
older campers treating boats with af¬ 
fection and good swimming procedures 
with respect, they will usually follow 
suit without question. 

Again, I believe that children have- 
a great need to try things out for them¬ 
selves, testing themselves against wind 
and water and a hard trail, and if this 
need can be satisfied, it will finally 
result in greater safety. For instance, 
an occasional chance to swim (with 
accompanying boat) beyond the usual 
bounds to some not-too-distant goal, 
will often satisfy this urge. Similarly, 
if campers who are good swimmers, 
are sometimes allowed to take out an 
old canoe and try stunts in it, freely 
testing both it and themselves, then 
they will not only be more at home in 
canoes but they will develop a real 
understanding of them and with it a 
readiness • to accept good practice in 
the use of boats. 

The more freedom that is granted 
to campers, however, the greater is the 
responsibility upon the shoulders of 
those in charge. In fact, it takes such 
courage to preserve the spirit of ad¬ 
venture that leaders can hardly be 
blamed if sometimes they prefer to 
smother it under “do’s and don’ts”. 
Behind the sense of freedom of a good 
camp there lies intensive preliminary 
work. The director and staff will have 
foreseen possible accidents and have 
already taken steps to guard against 
them. There will have been very care¬ 
ful planning of the waterfront, and 
careful consideration of programme so 
that small, rather than large, groups 
may embark on adventures together. 
Most important of all is the careful 
selection and training of staff. It is, 
perhaps, not too much to state that 
when the staff is very young and inex¬ 
perienced, many restrictions for the 
campers are necessary, but that the 


more mature and competent the coun¬ 
selors, the more can rules be dispensed 
with and zest for camping maintained. 

Here, in the training of Instructors, 
lies the chief Service of the Red Cros 
to Water Safety in Canada. We do not 
suggest that in a brief, thirty-hour 
course we can transform a novice into 
a wise and experienced counselor, but 
we do suggest that if a young instructor 
has learned to think in terms of safety 
—individual safety, group safety, water¬ 
front safety—and to think of it as part 
of the larger pattern of camp educa¬ 
tion, that we shall have safe and sane 
living in our camps and that the high 
adventure of the woods and the waters 
will not be lost. 

This is the first of a series of articles 
on services rendered by the Canadian 
Red Cross to Camping. For further 
information get in touch with the Red 
Cross Commissioner for your province, 
or the National Commissioner, 95 
Wellesley St., Toronto. 



The safety of a camp Waterfront 
depends in part upon the sound train¬ 
ing of the Swimming Instructors.

Canadian Camping 



The Editor Comments 


With this issue we' begin Volume II 
of “Canadian Camping”, and there is 
an inclination to do some stock-taking. 
How are we measuring up to our aim: 
“to present to camp directors and coun¬ 
selors, articles of timely interest on 
many phases of camp life, notes on 
events in provincial associations, discus¬ 
sions of new trends and developments, 
book reviews, an exchange of program 
and practical ideas and a selected list 
cf advertisers who cater to the camp 
clientele”? For the measure in which 
we are achieving our goal, we thank 
all those who have contributed articles, 
news items and book reviews. 

This is a cooperative venture, in 
■which we are all gladly sharing our 
ideas on camping. We would ask our 


readers to suggest writers and subjects 
for future issues. We would beg the 
provincial associations to send in items 
of news. Comments and criticisms will 
be appreciated. Only by hearing from 
you can we judge whether we are 
“hitting the mark”. ' 

“Canadian Camping” must be what 
its name implies. It must be truly 
Canadian, and it must deal with many 
and varied aspects of camping. It 
should never be dull, stuffy, unimagina¬ 
tive and- unprogressive, for it is con¬ 
cerned with youth and the out-of-doors 
and a great young country which “was 
built around camp fires”. Surely there 
lies the challenge and the inspiration 
to make this little magazine something 
worth while. 



This picture was taken at a special course for Camp Counselors conducted 
by the Water Safety Department of the Ontario Division Red Cross. 


Tcronlo, Canada, February, 1950

NOTJES 

from the I*rovinces 

BRITISH COLUMBIA 

The outstanding event to which the 
B.C. Camping Association is looking 
forward in 1950 is the Annual National 
Convention of the Canadian Associa¬ 
tion for Health, Physical Education 
and Recreation, \yhich is to. be held in 
Vancouver in June. Camping is to 
have an important part in the program 
of this convention, and Miss Anne Vail, 
our .National President, hopes to be 
present, as well as other outstanding 
camp leaders from the east. Miss Ger¬ 
trude Moore is chairing the committee 
on camping and is working on ideas 
for displays, films, workshops, etc. 

The Y.W.C.A., Y.M.C.A., Alexandra 
and Gordon Neighbourhood Houses 
ran day camps last summer and made 
valuable contribution to camping, as 
circumstances prevent so many children 
from being able to attend regular 
camps. 

Gordon House day camp program 
was ambitious and would seem to have 
achieved a real camping experience for 
the thirty-two boys and girls who at¬ 
tended for the month. They were able 
to secure a campsite on U.B.C. endow¬ 
ment land. There the children travel¬ 
led three days a week to clear bush, 
build their cabins, have- their camp¬ 
fires and occasional sleep-outs. The 
other two days were devoted to crafts 
in the a.m. at Gordon House and swim¬ 
ming instruction at Second Beach under 
the supervision of the Canadian Red 
Cross Society. 

ALBERTA 

From Alberta we have a most in¬ 
teresting article printed in this issue, 
“Camping —- Mountain Style”. This 
gives a colorful picture of what the 
Y.M.C.A. and Y.W.C.A. are doing. 
The Girl Guides, Boy Scouts and C.G. 


I.T. have many camps dotted over the 
province, by the shores of many small 
lakes, and we hope to be able to give 
interesting glimpses in later issues of 
prairie, as well as mountain-camping. 

ONTARIO 

The main item of interest in the 
Ontario Association is the forth-comin^ 
Camp Conference, March 10th and 
11 th, which the various committees, 
now at work, are planning to make 
“the best yet”. See more detailed an¬ 
nouncement of this Camp Conference 
on pages 16 and 17. 

The Committee on Research has 
compiled a bulletin for members on 
_ Know Your Camps”, giving some 
interesting facts and figures about On¬ 
tario camps. 

A few facts of interest. Did you 
know that: 

—There art: 114 camps and camp 
groups in the Ontario Camping Asso¬ 
ciation; 41% are private camps; 49% 
organization, and 10% “special”. 

—Boys’ camps outnumber girls’ 
camps two to one.. There are almost 
as many co-educational camps as there 
are girls’ camps. 

—The first camp in Ontario opened 
in 1893 and is the Y.M.C.A. Camp 
On-Da-Da-Waks at Golden Lake, On¬ 
tario. 

—Twenty-eight camps have been * 
opened since 1945. 

QUEBEC 

The Quebec Section has been con¬ 
cerned with courses and conferences. 
The McGill Extension Department 
offered us an opportunity to plan a 
course for the next ten weeks. Al¬ 
though the notice was short, a verv 
satisfactory series of lectures was or¬ 
ganized. Names familiar in the camp¬ 
ing field include: Miss Anne Vail, 
Miss Norah Bailey, Miss Dorothy Per- 
cival. Authorities -on health, camp 
management and arts and crafts, will 
speak on their specialties. 


14 


Canadian Camping 



Conference plans are well under way, 
with the dates set for March 31 - April 
1 / We would be glad to have people 
from other sections join us. The pro¬ 
gram is not completely outlined as yet, 
but if hard work and meetings pay off, 
the week-end should be very valuable. 

The regular monthly meetings have 
taken place with Dr. Allan Ross speak¬ 
ing on Health, Mr. Allan Mills, the 
radio singer on Camp Music and Dr. 
Wilson speaking on Camp generally. 

NEWFOUNDLAND 

Under the supervision of the Na¬ 
tional C.G.I.T. Committee, a camp 
project for Newfoundland girls’ leaders 
was sponsored last summer. At Mus- 
gravetown it was arranged to have two 
groups—one a ’teen age group carrying 
on the usual teen-age program; the 
other a leadership group to observe and 
assist. Each camper was encouraged 
to go back to her community to im¬ 
prove the quality of leadership in the 
home church. Their slogan was “Each 
one teach one”. 

At Lcwisport the campers were 


younger and the leadership phase ol the 
program became a course on “Looking 
toward Leadership”, 

Camping is decidedly in the pioneer¬ 
ing stage. At Musgravetown the camp¬ 
ers met for their program in the school 
house, where they ate their meals, 
cooked, sang, and had activities on 
windy or rainy days. Some of the 
campers commuted each' day from a 
nearby village; three lived in at their 
own homes; several were billeted, and 
ten lived in an unoccupied, unfurnish¬ 
ed house which they called “The Wig¬ 
wam”. Lack of a real camp site de¬ 
tracted from the fun and the benefit 
of community living, but in spite of 
this a fine spirit was developed. 

e 

The twenty-first National Conven¬ 
tion of the American Camping Associ¬ 
ation will be held in St. Louis, Mo., 
February 15th - 18th. The convention 
headquarters will be Hotel Jefferson, 
and the chairman is J. Edward Dodds, 
Y.M.C.A., 1528 Locust Street, St. 

Louis, Mo.

start Feb. 6th, continuing through Feb¬ 
ruary, two nights a week. 

Toronto: A course will start on 
Monday, February 27th, at the Ontario 
College of Education at 7 p.m., and 
will run every Monday and Wednesday 
evening until March 29. 

Kingston: An intensive course in 
the Easter holidays will be held at the 
Queen’s University pool April 11th to 
loth. 

Port Hope: A course similar to that 
at Kingston will be held in Port Hope 
during the Easter holidays. 

Courses are also being planned for 
May or June in Cornwall, Simcoe 
County, the Lakehead, Windsor, Lon¬ 
don, Thorold, Sudbury and Petawawa. 

For further information, contact the 
Water Safety Department, Ontario 
Division Red Cross, 621 Jarvis Street, 
Toronto.

ed and directed for twenty-five years 
by Miss Ferna G. Halliday, has been

Ontario Camping 
Association Conference 

“It will give me great pleasure to 
attend your Annual Conference on 
March 10 and 11”, wrote Mr. Bernard 
S. Mason in replying to the invitation 
of the Ontario section of the Canadian 
Camping Association. “It is many 
years since I have visited Canada and 
I understand that the camping move¬ 
ment has expanded rapidly during the 
last decade.” 

Bernard Mason needs no introduc¬ 
tion to camper, counselor, or camp 
director. As the author of many books 
on camping and woodcraft he has 
made a vital contribution to the whole 
movement. His appearance at the On¬ 
tario Conference, which is again to be 
held at the Central Y.W.C.A. in Tor¬ 
onto, will high-light a stimulating pro¬ 
gramme. 

Other outstanding speakers secured 
by the Conference Committee are Mr. 
Sidney Hazelton, writer of the popular 
and practical “Camp Aquatic Pro¬ 
gram”, and Mr. Bradford Sears of the 
New York School of Forestry, an auth¬ 
ority on camp structures and campsite 
development. Discussion groups will be 
directed largely by Canadians promi¬ 
nent in the camping field. 

While provision has been made for 
food services at moderate cost during 
the entire conference, only one formal 
banquet will be held. The guest speaker 
for this occasion will be Mr. Leo Dolan, 
Director of the Canadian Government 
Travel Bureau. Mr. Dolan'is a forceful 
and entertaining speaker who will dis¬ 
cuss the relationship of camping to the 
work of his department. 

A warm invitation is extended to 
camping people in other provinces to 
come to Toronto to share your experi¬ 
ences and problems with us, and to find 
inspiration and guidance in the mess¬ 
ages which will be brought to us by 
the camping authorities. Detailed in¬ 
formation can be obtained by writing to 

The Ontario Camping Association 
236 Bloor St. West, Toronto 5. 

J. H. Passmore, 
Conference Co-Chairman.

ON THE BEAM: Toronto Y.M.C.A., 
Camp Tonakclo (India) Committee, 
222 Front St. East, Toronto. Joint 
chairmen, Taylor Statten and Dr. 
Chas. E. Hendry. Price, 50c or five 
copies for $2.00. 

This book of devotional and inspira¬ 
tional stories for boys has been publish¬ 
ed to meet an urgent demand on the 
part of teachers, church leaders, scout¬ 
masters, Y.M.C.A. secretaries, and 
others, and is Intended for the use of 
boys from twelve to fifteen years of age. 
There arc sixty-six stories suitable for 
brief club or camp devotions,' and 
thirty-five outstanding men have con¬ 
tributed their best and most inspiring 
stories, many of the names being very 
familiar to readers of “Canadian 
Camping”. 

Of particular interest is the fact that 
the total profits from the sale of this 
book go to help “Camp Tonakela” in 
India, which was established in 1936, 
and serves the boys and girls from one 
of the world’s most densely-crowded 
cities-—-Madras. ‘ 

The camp gets its name from Mrs. 
Taylor Statten, who is affectionately 


known at Wapomeo as “Tonakelo”. 
Many Canadian campers and counsel¬ 
ors have had a share in the magnificent 
camp work being done by Wallace 
Forgic in far-off India. “On the Beam” 
is a fine book for campers of either the 
East or the West. 

IN SEARCH OF OURSELVES: By 

Len Peterson and Dr. J. D. M. Grif¬ 
fin. Published by McClelland and 
Stewart, Toronto, 1949; price, $1.25 
for set of 35c each. 

This is a set of four booklets: 1. Sex 
Education. 2. Brotherly Hatred. 3. 
The Careful Boy. 4. Adolescent Rebel¬ 
lion. They were presented as a series 
of broadcasts over C.B.C. and each one 
dramatised the ease -history of-an indi¬ 
vidual with a personality problem, fol¬ 
lowed up by the professional analysis 
by a psychiatrist. These broadcasts 
formed the basis of many discussion 
groups throughout the Dominion. 

Each pamphlet contains the script 
originally prepared for radio by Len 
Peterson, noted Canadian author and 
playright, a commentary by Dr. J. D. 
M. Griffin, Medical Director of the

National Committee on Mental Hy¬

The pamphlets deal specifically with 
problems of youth and adolescence, and 
can be recommended not only for sheer 
entertainment, but for down-to-earth 
thought-provoking situations. Adoles¬ 
cence often is a painful, unhappy ex¬ 
perience. Reading particularly “Adol¬ 
escent Rebellion” will help us to under¬ 
stand the rebellious spirit of adolescent 
girls and boys and make us more eager 
to help our ’teen-age campers through 
their difficult growing-up days. 

THE CHILDREN’S BOOK OF 
TREES: By Leonard L. Knott: 
pub., Editorial Associates, 1222 Uni¬ 
versity Street, Montreal; price, $1.00. 

This book about Canada’s trees is 
most attractively illustrated with clever 
and amusing pictures, and is designed 
to make children aware of the beauty 
and usefulness of trees. It stresses also 
in a picturesque and impressive man¬ 
ner, the tremendous importance of our 
forests and how essential they are in 
preserving the good Canadian way of 
life. The story deals with the trees 
that are native to our country and 
points out some of their greatest ene¬ 
mies, the greatest, of course, being fire. 
This is a valuable book to add to a 
camp library or to recommend to any 
counselor or camper. 

LIFT YOUR VOICES: 'Canadian 
Girls in Training Office, 299 Queen 
St. West, Toronto; price, 50c. 

This is a new song book published 
by the Department of Christian Edu¬ 
cation, Canadian Council of Churches. 
This book is a splendid supplement to 
the familiar, much-used book, “The 
Treasure Book of Songs”. It contains 
over one hundred songs and hymns 
with words and music—songs that boys 
“arrad "girls'will “enjoy. Tt is “dune up in 
convenient pocket size and is offered 
at a very low price.

“CAMPING.AND WOODCRAFT”, 
by Horace Kephert, published by 
Macmillan Co., 70 Bond St., Tor¬ 
onto. Reprinted Dec. 1947, pp. 479. 

Many folks arc interested in organ¬ 
ized camping nowadays, a lot of them 
thinking of it as something quite new. 
This book is proof that camping is 
well nigh a half century old. It is also 
a demonstration that camping has had 
a sound literature during all of that 
time. 

It is an omnibus on camping. Revi¬ 
sions have kept it relatively up to date. 
Since the plains and the wilderness 
and the lakes and sea change very 
little, methods of meeting change little 
too. 

For those with questions and prob¬ 
lems, the book has tested answers and 
solutions. For those who want to learn 
about all the details of camping, this 
text will serve as well as it has since 
its original appearance in two volumes 
in 1906.

TRADING

| PIERRE’S WISDOM 

Dat fello, Pierre, has been running 
around a bit of late, getting his ear 
into other necks of the bush. He was 
in the Trading Post the other day, 
sounding off about what he had heard 
of school camps. Of course, he is very 
taken with the idea, since the only 
school he attended and the only 
“lamin’he has, was acquired in the 
school of the bush. 

Pierre is of the opinion that it will 
be very interesting to watch the devel¬ 
opment of school camping in Canada. 
He realizes that educators here may be 
more conservative than their opposite

numbers in the States, but since many 
of them have been raised on or near 
the farms, that they may do a better 
job of it once they get at it. 

Pierre’s wisdom is that of the bush 
and the variety of life that dwells 
therein. School camping will give boys 
and girls a chance to learn about it first 
hand. Pierre feels that it is important 
.that these young people, who dwell for 
the most part in the city, should know 
about the efforts being made to con¬ 
serve and restore the native life of the 
bush. Reports he had had of school 
camps lead him to believe that they 
are a fine method of showing the 
“kids”.

Pierre would like to know about 
camps near the cities which have living 
quarters which could be used for school 
camping projects. He thinks that there 
might be quite a few which could be 
made available for the late fall and 
early spring- months.--There are-prob¬ 
ably fewer which could be used in the 
winter time. 

—C.R.B. 


RED LETTER DAYS 

Camp Alexandra Girls’ Camp in 
British Columbia last summer develop¬ 
ed an interesting theme: That of im¬ 
personating the characters of a book, 
poem or legend each day. There was 
Swiss Family Robinson Day, Alice in 
Wonderland Day, Tom Sawyer Day, 
Indian Legend Day, and The Trail of 
"93, and others. Activities for that day 
revolved around the story they were 
enacting. This provided incentive for 
evening skits, day program, dress-up, 
etc. Indirectly, the girls became inter¬ 
ested in the old familiar stories and 
legends, too often omitted in these days 
cd competition with the comics and 
movies.

In Tighter Vein 

Once there was a camper 
And it was her boastful aim, 

All life-saving tests to pass, 

And thus achieve much fame. 

Her “Buddy” practised with her 
And clutched her with such vim, 
She shrieked: “I much prefer to drown 
Than be saved by means so grim”. 

—M.S.E. 


Prospective camp director: “Well, 
how do you like this property”? 

Wife: “It is simply marvellous. The 
view just leaves me speechless”. 

Director: “Then we’ll certainly buv 
it”! • 


Small camper (to counselor on por¬ 
tage) : “Say, can I help you”? 

Counselor: (struggling with canoe 
and pack sack) : “A little shrimp like 
you? What could you do?” 

Camper: “Well, I could do the 
groaning while you carry the canoe”.
